prompt.context: John Burnett, the Chief Merchandize Officer at Premium Home, remarked to himself as he read the past year's annual results: 'This economy has destroyed our profits.' The CEO and Board are looking to him for ideas, but he is unsure how to prioritize various options. Should he reduce prices to increase sales? Should he switch from domestic to foreign suppliers to reduce costs? Premium Home is a retailer specializing in selling home furnishings and accessories. Its target audience is the medium to high-end market (median customer household annual income of $130-$200k). The company image stresses style, modernity, and luxury. It operates 800 stores across the US and competes with department stores (e.g., Macy's) and specialized chains (e.g., Crate & Barrel, Williams & Sonoma). It has two divisions: Home & Kitchen (dinnerware, kitchen supplies, bedding) and Furniture (couches, dining room chairs, bedroom sets). In the last year, revenue is down 50%, driven by customer unemployment and trade-down to mass merchandisers (Walmart, Target). Premium Home uses two warehouses (one per division); warehouse space is rented but uses internal labor. Products are stored at the warehouse until needed by stores, then shipped via a third-party logistics company. Premium Home does NOT own its fleet.
prompt.question: John has two potential actions to improve profitability: (1) decrease all prices by 5% assuming a 30% increase in sales volume, and (2) switch to foreign suppliers for up to 50% of products. Please evaluate these options and advise John on what he should do.

clarifying_info.q: What evidence do we have that a 5% price cut leads to a 30% volume increase?
clarifying_info.a: In a recent promotion for a new line of celebrity branded cookware, a 5% decrease in price resulted in a 30% increase in sales volume.

clarifying_info.q: Where do suppliers currently deliver product?
clarifying_info.a: Domestic suppliers pay for delivery of product to the Premium Home warehouse. Lead times are currently 3-4 days on average.

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of products could be sourced from foreign suppliers?
clarifying_info.a: If there is a compelling case, the company believes it could buy up to 50% of products from foreign suppliers.

clarifying_info.q: What are the trade-offs of foreign suppliers?
clarifying_info.a: Foreign suppliers offer cheaper product cost due to lower wage rates and elimination of the middleman wholesaler. However, there are tariffs, customs handling challenges, longer lead times (2-3 months), and the need to hold more safety stock inventory.

exhibits.title: 2009 Revenue Statement ($Ms USD)
exhibits.shows: Income statement broken down by Home & Kitchen and Furniture divisions, showing Revenue, Cost of Goods (includes warehouse and transportation), Gross Profit, SG&A (fixed costs), Net Profit, and Total Units Sold.

exhibits.title: Breakdown of Total Cost of Goods ($Ms)
exhibits.shows: COGS breakdown into three cost components — product cost only, warehouse handling/storage costs, and shipping/handling from warehouse to stores — split by Home & Kitchen and Furniture divisions.

exhibits.title: Current Per Unit Data
exhibits.shows: Per unit cost breakdown for each division, showing total units sold, average product cost per unit from domestic suppliers, warehouse/handling/storage cost per unit, and shipping/handling from warehouse to stores per unit.

exhibits.title: Data for Switching to Foreign Suppliers
exhibits.shows: Cost data for foreign supplier scenario, showing average per unit product cost, international shipping and handling cost from supplier to Premium Home warehouse, tariff as a percentage of product cost, and additional millions of units needed in inventory due to increased lead times — split by division.

exhibits.title: Data on Competitors ($Ms)
exhibits.shows: Comparative financials for Premium Home and three unnamed competitors, including Revenue, COGS, Gross Margin, SG&A, Net Profit, number of stores, number of suppliers, and cost of capital.

framework: Assess current profitability baseline: revenue, COGS, gross profit, SG&A, and net profit by division
Evaluate Option 1 — price reduction: calculate new revenue and COGS given 5% price cut and 30% volume increase; assess gross profit impact

Evaluate Option 2 — foreign supplier switch: calculate per-unit cost savings net of tariffs and international shipping; estimate inventory carrying cost increase from longer lead times; compute net P&L impact
Compare gross profit improvement vs. additional inventory costs for each option
Identify short- and long-term risks for each recommended action
Challenge assumptions and flag factors warranting further investigation
Benchmark against competitors on gross margin, SG&A efficiency, and supplier base

questions.prompt: Question 1: Calculate the impact on gross profit if Premium Home decreases all prices by 5% and assumes a 30% increase in sales volume.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate new revenue using reduced price and higher volume for each division, then recalculate COGS (variable cost per unit x new units), and derive the new gross profit. Base case price per unit: Home & Kitchen = $60, Furniture = $1,000. Note that COGS per unit = $45 (H&K) and $700 (Furniture) — these are variable costs that scale with volume. SG&A is fixed and does not change. A strong answer shows the calculation cleanly and interprets whether the strategy is worthwhile.

math.setup: Base: H&K 50M units at $60 price, $45 variable COGS/unit; Furniture 1M units at $1,000 price, $700 COGS/unit. New scenario: 5% price cut, 30% volume increase for both divisions.
steps: New net profit: $1,105M - $1,480M (fixed SG&A) = -$375M (vs -$430M base, improvement of $55M)
math.answer: Gross profit improves by $55M (from $1,050M to $1,105M); net loss improves from -$430M to -$375M. The company remains unprofitable.

questions.prompt: Question 2: What are the potential cost savings of switching to foreign suppliers? (Assume up to 50% of units can be switched.)
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate: (a) new total variable cost per unit from foreign suppliers including product cost, international shipping, tariff, domestic warehouse and shipping costs; (b) savings per unit vs. current domestic cost; (c) total P&L savings on the 50% of units switched; (d) additional inventory carrying cost from longer lead times. Strong answer nets out carrying costs to show true benefit. Tariff is calculated on product cost only.

math.setup: 50% of current units switched to foreign suppliers. H&K: 50M x 50% = 25M units affected; Furniture: 1M x 50% = 0.5M units affected. Warehouse/storage and domestic shipping costs remain unchanged for switched units.
steps: H&K foreign variable cost per unit: product $20 + intl shipping $5 + tariff ($20 x 10% = $2) + warehouse $3 + domestic shipping $2 = $32... wait, casebook uses warehouse $2 and shipping $2 in solution: product $20 + intl shipping $5 + tariff $2 + warehouse $2 + domestic shipping $2 = $31
Furniture foreign variable cost per unit: product $495 + intl shipping $50 + tariff ($495 x 26% = $128.7) + warehouse $5 + domestic shipping $5 = $683.7
Total gross P&L savings: $350M + $8.1M = $358.2M (before inventory cost)
Additional inventory units needed: H&K 2.04M units, Furniture 0.08M units
H&K extra inventory cost: 2.04M units x $31/unit = ~$63.2M
Furniture extra inventory cost: 0.08M units x $683.7/unit = ~$54.7M
Total extra inventory on balance sheet: $63.2M + $54.7M = $117.9M
Inventory carrying cost (at 10% cost of capital): $117.9M x 10% = $11.8M per year
math.answer: Gross cost savings of ~$358M; after accounting for annual inventory carrying cost of ~$11.8M, net annual benefit is approximately $346M. This is significantly larger than the price-cut option's $55M gross profit improvement.

questions.prompt: Question 3: What are some of the short- and long-term risks in implementing your recommendations?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify risks specific to each option. Strong answers are organized (e.g., by price cut risks vs. foreign supplier risks), cover brand, operational, competitive, and financial dimensions, and show business judgment about which risks are most material.

questions.prompt: Question 4: Are there any assumptions Premium Home made that you would challenge or factors that merit further consideration?
questions.guidance: Candidate should critically evaluate the assumptions underpinning the analysis and identify missing information. Strong answers address elasticity assumptions, quality assumptions, and competitive dynamics.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the risks of the two recommended strategies (price cut and foreign supplier switch)?

categories.name: Price Cut Risks
ideas: Brand image damage — luxury/premium positioning may be undermined by discounting
Supplier capacity — can domestic suppliers provide 30% more units?
Logistics capacity — can third-party logistics handle the extra volume?
Competitor response — rivals may match price cuts, eliminating the volume gain
Elasticity assumption — 5% cut on celebrity cookware may not generalize to all product categories
Upside potential not explored — what if raising prices was also considered?

categories.name: Foreign Supplier Risks
ideas: Brand image damage — customers may perceive foreign-made goods as lower quality
Inventory stockouts — longer lead times increase stockout risk
Warehouse capacity — can warehouses hold the additional safety stock inventory?
Staff capability — can warehouse staff manage higher inventory volumes?
Skills gap — does the company have expertise to manage imports (tariffs, customs, etc.)?
Lead time volatility — international supply chains have unknown variability
Responsiveness — company cannot respond to market changes as quickly with 2-3 month lead times
Quality risk — foreign products may not match domestic supplier quality standards

recommendation: Pursue the foreign supplier switch (up to 50% of products) as the primary lever — it generates ~$358M in gross cost savings versus only ~$55M gross profit improvement from the price cut
The price cut strategy improves profitability modestly but the company remains deeply unprofitable; the foreign supplier switch offers a far larger financial impact
Consider the price cut selectively (e.g., for categories where the celebrity cookware elasticity is validated) rather than company-wide
risks: Price cut risks brand equity with the $130-200k household income target customer; competitor response could neutralize volume gains
Foreign supplier switch introduces supply chain complexity, quality risk, and requires new organizational capabilities in import management; inventory carrying costs partially offset savings
Neither option alone closes the $430M net loss gap; SG&A rationalization (company has 5,000 suppliers vs. competitors' 2,000-3,000 — supplier consolidation may reduce costs) deserves attention
next_steps: Validate price elasticity assumption across all product categories before a company-wide price cut
Pilot the foreign supplier switch in one product category to test lead time management and quality before scaling to 50%
Benchmark SG&A — Premium Home's $1,480M SG&A vs. competitor range of $930M-$1,400M suggests significant overhead reduction opportunity
Explore supplier consolidation — Premium Home has 5,000 suppliers versus 2,000-3,000 for profitable competitors; consolidation could improve purchasing leverage and reduce administrative costs
